newsitem.title: USA: American Cyanamid settles price-fixing charges. [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: American Cyanamid settles price-fixing charges. [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects spelling of company name throughout from American Cyanimid to American Cyanamid.)
American Cyanamid has agreed to pay $7.3 million to settle charges that it fixed prices for herbicides and insecticides, the federal and state governments said Thursday.
The Federal Trade Comission and all 50 states said the price-fixing began in 1989 and ended in 1994, about the time American Cyanamid was acquired by American Home Products Corp.

In 1995 American Cyanamid sold more than $1 billion of the products involved in the settlement -- soybean broadleaf herbicides, soybean grass herbicides, corn soil insecticides, and cotton grass insecticides.
The settlement must be approved by a federal court. The $7.3 million will be split among the 50 states and the District of Columbia.
American Cyanamid offered farm chemical dealers rebates of
up to 12 percent -- but only if they sold the products at or
During the time of the price-fixing, the FTC said, dealers overwhelmingly accepted the rebates. American Cyanamid signed written agreements with 2,500 dealers for the rebates.
A 4-1 majority of the FTC found that antitrust law prohibits companies from limiting price competition by offering such rebates.
The lone dissenter, Roscoe Starek III, said he believed American Cyanamid's actions were not illegal.
In a statement, American Home Products said it terminated the rebates when it acquired American Cyanamid, but it defended the rebates as legal.

"American Cyanamid believes its promotional programs were pro-competitive and lawful," the Parsippany, N.J., company said in a statement. "In order to avoid the burden and expense of litigation over a program that is no longer in effect, American Home Products agreed to settle these matters."
